security.metaTitle: Security: what ExoSeal does and does not protect | ExoSeal
security.metaDescription: ExoSeal's public threat model: what end-to-end encryption protects against, what it does not, and how to verify every claim yourself.
security.title: What is protected and what is not.
security.intro: A security tool that only lists strengths is not credible. This is the full threat model: what ExoSeal protects against, where it ends and how you check everything yourself.

a.name: Database or backup leaks
a.text: Only ciphertext is stored. Secrets are single-use and short-lived.

b.name: Curious operators
b.text: Whoever reads the database or logs finds no key, no plaintext and no IP addresses.

c.name: Link preview bots
c.text: Slack, Teams or Outlook only fetch links. Opening needs a click on a button, so a bot consumes nothing.

d.name: Mistyped passwords
d.text: The passphrase is checked in the browser before the reply is fetched and deleted.

e.name: Swapped public keys
e.text: The customer link carries a fingerprint of the key. If it does not match, the browser stops.

f.name: Parallel opening
f.text: Opening and answering are single database statements. With 30 to 40 parallel attempts exactly one wins.

g.name: Script injection
g.text: Strict Content-Security-Policy with a nonce per request and no external sources.

h.name: Foreign pages and other subdomains
h.text: The server accepts writing calls only from its own origin (Sec-Fetch-Site, Origin). A foreign or hacked page under the same main domain cannot create or delete anything in your name.

i.name: Overload and a full database
i.text: Rate limits count signed-in users one by one and everyone else by IP. Every user has a quota (500 running links, 200 running requests), so a hijacked account cannot fill the database.

a.name: A tampered server
a.text: The encrypting code comes from the server. Whoever takes over the server can ship modified code. That is why ExoSeal is open source and self-hostable. For very high stakes use a native tool such as age or GPG.

b.name: A short passphrase
b.text: For requests the wrapped private key is stored encrypted on the server. 600,000 iterations slow guessing down, but a short passphrase will still fall. Use a long sentence.

c.name: A forgotten passphrase
c.text: There is no recovery. The reply is gone.

d.name: A compromised device
d.text: Malware, shoulder surfing or clipboard managers on either side.

e.name: Metadata
e.text: The server knows that a request exists, when it was created, answered and opened, and who owns it, and which user created a link and when. It does not know the recipient or the content. The reverse proxy sees IP addresses unless you turn logging off.

f.name: The full link in the wrong hands
f.text: Whoever opens the complete link before the recipient wins. If the recipient finds the link used up, something is wrong.

g.name: A stolen session
g.text: The session lasts a fixed 8 hours. "Sign out" deletes the cookie in the browser; the server cannot end a stolen session early. The cookie is HttpOnly and the strict CSP stops scripts from reading it.

security.verifyIntro: You do not have to take our word for it. Three ways to verify every claim.

a.name: Read the source
a.text: Encryption lives in the frontend, storage rules in the backend. Both are open under AGPL-3.0 and short enough to read in an afternoon.

b.name: Look in the browser
b.text: Open the developer tools, Network tab. When you open a link, nothing after the # ever goes to the server. The browser decides that, not us.

c.name: Run it yourself
c.text: With a compose file and your own login provider, ExoSeal runs on your server. Then trust depends only on you.

security.ctaText: The most common questions are answered, and the guides show every step.

compare.metaTitle: Comparison: ExoSeal, email, chat, password managers | ExoSeal
compare.metaDescription: An honest comparison: passwords by email or chat, password managers, age or GPG, and ExoSeal. Where ExoSeal is better and where it is not.
compare.title: How ExoSeal compares.
compare.intro: No tool fits everywhere. Here you see where ExoSeal is stronger, where another tool fits better and why.
compare.betterIntro: We tell you honestly when you should not use ExoSeal.

a.name: Highest stakes
a.text: Against a tampered server only a native tool such as age or GPG helps, because no code comes from a server there.

b.name: Lasting team access
b.text: If several people need a password for a long time, it belongs in a password manager. ExoSeal is for handing something over once.

c.name: Large files
c.text: ExoSeal is meant for text up to 50,000 characters, not for files.

compare.ctaText: Read the threat model and the guides, then decide.

openSource.metaTitle: Open source: self-host ExoSeal under AGPL-3.0 | ExoSeal
openSource.metaDescription: ExoSeal is open source under AGPL-3.0. View the source, run it yourself with Docker and contribute.
openSource.title: Open, so you do not have to believe.
openSource.intro: All of ExoSeal's code is freely readable. Anyone who uses a tool for secrets should be able to check what it does, and to run it themselves.
openSource.licenseIntro: ExoSeal is licensed under the GNU Affero General Public License 3.0 (AGPL-3.0).

a.name: Use and operate
a.text: You may use ExoSeal freely, also commercially, on your own server.

b.name: Modify
b.text: You may adapt and extend the code.

c.name: Stay open
c.text: Whoever offers a modified version as a network service must publish the changes too.

openSource.hostText: One compose file, an OpenID Connect login provider and a reverse proxy are enough. Backend, database and cache run in Docker, and the backend is not reachable from the internet.

a.name: Frontend
a.text: Next.js and React, encryption in the browser with Web Crypto.

b.name: Backend
b.text: C# on .NET 10, only the backend talks to the database.

c.name: Data
c.text: PostgreSQL for secrets and requests, Valkey for short-lived counters.

openSource.joinText: Bugs, ideas and improvements are welcome. The contribution guide and the public repository arrive with the first release. Until then the changelog shows the current state.

e1.title: First stable release
e1.text: ExoSeal is released as open source (AGPL-3.0): ready-made Docker images, a documented update path, optional notification of new pages to search engines (IndexNow) and a tested setup behind Cloudflare, Traefik and CrowdSec.
